note:
ID clinic, new pt visit, referred by PCP for fever x5 days after intl travel.
Pt: 44-year-old male.

HPI
- fever x5 days, Tmax 102.6 F at home, chills, drenching night sweats, HA, diffuse myalgias
- loose stools 3-4/day x3 days, mild lower abd cramping, poor appetite
- returned 2 wks ago from 3 wk work trip to Cambodia and Vietnam. Ate street food, got mosquito bites. No freshwater swimming, no animal exposure.
- hospitalized abroad x3 days for dengue fever (NS1 pos per pt), got IV fluids + IV ceftriaxone, no records brought. Pt first said admission was 2 wks ago. Correction, it was 3 wks ago, before the flight home, per his d/c paper.
- malaria ppx: pt first said he took doxy daily the whole trip. Correction, bottle in hand is atovaquone-proguanil 1 tab daily, started 1 day pre-travel, stopped on day of return (should have continued 7 days after return).
- denies cough, SOB, CP, dysuria, rash, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting, hematochezia, melena, jaundice
- no sick contacts at home

PMH: T2DM, HTN, HLD, obesity
Allergy: sulfa -> rash
Meds: metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, omeprazole 40 mg daily (started abroad, pt unsure why), acetaminophen 650 mg q6h PRN
Social: lives w/ wife, 1-2 beers/wk, never smoker

Vitals: Temp 102.4 F, HR 76, BP 108/68, RR 18, SpO2 97% RA, wt 98 kg. Relative bradycardia for temp.
Exam: ill-appearing but nontoxic, dry MM. No scleral icterus, no LAD. Neck supple, no meningismus. Lungs CTAB. RRR, no murmur. Abd soft, spleen tip palpable, mild diffuse tenderness worse RLQ, no rebound or guarding, no hepatomegaly. Skin: faint blanching salmon-colored macules x3 on lower chest/upper abd (c/w rose spots), no petechiae, no eschar. Ext: no edema, prior R forearm IV site healed, no erythema.

Labs (drawn by PCP this AM): WBC 3.4, Hgb 12.8, Plt 112, Na 133, K 4.1, Cr 1.4 (baseline 0.9), AST 82, ALT 76, glucose 238, A1c 8.2
Malaria RDT in clinic today: neg. UA neg. CXR 2-view at PCP: clear.

Impression
1. Febrile illness after SE Asia travel, suspect typhoid fever (fever, relative bradycardia, rose spots, leukopenia, mild transaminitis, spleen tip). Ddx malaria despite neg RDT given incomplete ppx, dengue recurrence, C diff after ceftriaxone abroad, less likely.
2. AKI, likely prerenal from dehydration (Cr 1.4, baseline 0.9)
3. T2DM w/ hyperglycemia, HTN, HLD

Mgmt
- start azithromycin 500 mg PO daily x7 days after blood cx drawn
- blood cx x2 today before 1st dose; malaria thick/thin smears now and q12h x2 more; stool cx, stool O&P, C diff PCR; repeat CBC and CMP in 48 h; abd US for spleen and liver
- stop omeprazole (no clear indication, PPI raises enteric infection risk)
- hold metformin while febrile w/ diarrhea and AKI; check fingerstick glucose BID
- decrease lisinopril 20 mg -> 10 mg daily until Cr back to baseline
- continue amlodipine 5 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, recheck LFTs w/ labs
- acetaminophen 650 mg q6h PRN fever, no NSAIDs (AKI)
- PO fluids/ORS 2-3 L/day
- ED precautions reviewed: persistent vomiting, confusion, severe abd pain, black stools
- f/u in clinic 48 h, ID will call pt w/ smear and cx results. If smears pos or clinically worse -> ED for IV tx. Work note given, stay home until afebrile 48 h.
summary: A 44-year-old male with T2DM, HTN and HLD presented with five days of fever, chills, night sweats and loose stools after a three-week trip to Cambodia and Vietnam, including a dengue fever admission abroad three weeks ago. His malaria prophylaxis was stopped on the day of return, and he denied cough, dysuria and neck stiffness. He was febrile with relative bradycardia, faint rose spots, a palpable spleen tip, leukopenia, mild transaminitis and a creatinine of 1.4 above baseline; malaria RDT and chest x-ray were negative. The impression was suspected typhoid fever with prerenal AKI. Plan includes azithromycin, cultures, malaria smears and stool studies, holding metformin, stopping omeprazole, reducing lisinopril, and follow-up in 48 hours.

This 82-year-old male returns to the nephrology clinic for follow-up of nephrotic syndrome. A kidney biopsy two months ago showed membranous nephropathy, and his anti-PLA2R antibody was positive. Over the past three weeks he has noticed more swelling in both legs and foamy urine, and his weight at home is up about 2 kg. He denies shortness of breath, orthopnea, chest pain, gross hematuria, flank pain, and fever. He has not used any NSAIDs or herbal supplements. His past history includes hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Current medications are lisinopril 10 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and he reports taking them reliably.

Vitals today show blood pressure 148/84, heart rate 72, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and weight 84.6 kg, compared with 82.4 kg at the last visit. On exam he is comfortable and speaks in full sentences. Jugular venous pressure is not elevated, the lungs are clear, and the heart sounds are regular. There is 2+ pitting edema of both legs to the knees and no ascites.

Labs drawn this morning show creatinine 1.3, eGFR 52, potassium 4.6, serum albumin 2.4 g/dL, LDL 162, and a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 6.8 g/g, which is increased from 5.2 last visit.

My impression is persistent nephrotic syndrome from membranous nephropathy with volume overload, along with hypertension that is above goal. His kidney function is stable. I increased lisinopril to 20 mg daily for better blood pressure control and antiproteinuric effect, and I will check a basic metabolic panel in one week because of the potassium. Furosemide will go up from 40 mg daily to 40 mg twice daily for the edema. He will continue atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, follow a 2 g sodium diet, and keep avoiding NSAIDs. Because membranous nephropathy in an older adult can be associated with malignancy, I ordered a CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. The albumin is low enough that we will revisit prophylactic anticoagulation at the next visit. He will return in two weeks with a repeat urine protein-to-creatinine ratio.

note:
Visit type: audio-only telephone visit, no video available. Patient identity confirmed with two identifiers and verbal consent for telephone care obtained. The patient is at home alone in a private room.

Reason for visit: seasonal allergic rhinitis flare in a 51-year-old female.

History reported by patient: She has had about 3 weeks of sneezing fits, a clear runny nose, nasal congestion, itchy watery eyes, and post-nasal drip, worst in the mornings and when she mows the lawn. This began when the tree pollen season started and follows the same pattern every spring. She denies fever, facial pain, wheezing, shortness of breath, or loss of smell. She has no known drug allergies.

Over-the-counter use: for the past 2 weeks she has taken diphenhydramine 50 mg at bedtime to help with sleep and her nasal symptoms, and pseudoephedrine 60 mg up to three times daily during the day. She says the diphenhydramine leaves her groggy in the morning.

Other history: hypertension, hypothyroidism, GERD, and depression. Prescribed medications are amlodipine 5 mg daily, levothyroxine, omeprazole 20 mg daily, and sertraline 50 mg daily. She first said she takes levothyroxine 100 mcg daily, then read the bottle during the call and corrected this to 75 mcg daily.

Alcohol: she first said she has a couple of glasses of wine most nights, and then, when asked directly, said it is closer to five glasses of wine every night, with more on weekends, and she has not had a drink-free day in months. She denies tremor, hallucinations, or seizures on days she drinks less. Her AUDIT-C score by phone was 11.

Pregnancy status: her last menstrual period was about four months ago, with irregular cycles for a year, consistent with perimenopause. She is sexually active with her husband and uses no contraception. A home urine pregnancy test this morning was negative.

Home measurements: blood pressure 148/94 on her home cuff, repeat 144/90, pulse 84, home temperature 98.4 F. She has no pulse oximeter.

Recent labs from 2 weeks ago: TSH 6.8, AST 88, ALT 54, hemoglobin 12.9, platelets 148, MCV 101.

Observation by phone: she speaks in full sentences with a mildly nasal quality to her voice, no audible wheeze, and no cough or hoarseness during the 20 minute call. She is coherent and oriented.

Impression: seasonal allergic rhinitis, poorly controlled on a sedating over-the-counter regimen. Hypertension above goal at home, likely worsened by pseudoephedrine. Hypothyroidism that is under-replaced with a TSH of 6.8. Alcohol use disorder with elevated transaminases and macrocytosis. Pregnancy is very unlikely given the negative test and perimenopausal status, so there are no pregnancy-related prescribing restrictions at this time.

Management:
- Start fluticasone propionate nasal spray 50 mcg per spray, 2 sprays in each nostril once daily.
- Start loratadine 10 mg once daily; it is non-sedating and preferred given her alcohol use.
- Stop diphenhydramine because of sedation and its additive effect with alcohol.
- Stop pseudoephedrine because of her blood pressure.
- Increase levothyroxine from 75 mcg daily to 88 mcg daily and recheck TSH in 6 to 8 weeks.
- Start thiamine 100 mg daily and folic acid 1 mg daily.
- Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily, and sertraline 50 mg daily. Keep a home blood pressure log and call if readings are above 160/100.
- Alcohol: brief counseling given, advised not to stop abruptly on her own, referral to addiction medicine placed, and she prefers counseling before discussing medication options. Hepatic panel in 4 weeks.
- She will call before starting any new medication if her periods return or she thinks she could be pregnant.
- Follow up by video in 4 weeks, sooner for wheezing, fever, facial pain lasting more than 10 days, or shakiness.

A home pregnancy test was negative and she is perimenopausal, so pregnancy did not restrict prescribing. Home blood pressure was 148/94 and recent TSH was 6.8 with elevated AST and ALT. The impression was poorly controlled allergic rhinitis, hypertension above goal, under-replaced hypothyroidism and alcohol use disorder. Plan is fluticasone and loratadine, stopping diphenhydramine and pseudoephedrine, increasing levothyroxine to 88 mcg, starting thiamine and folic acid, addiction medicine referral, and video follow-up in 4 weeks.

Hospital day 3 progress note for a 75-year-old female admitted with acute kidney injury from dehydration after four days of poor oral intake with a presumed viral gastroenteritis. A professional Spanish interpreter was used by video for the entire visit, and the patient confirmed her understanding using teach-back.

Overnight there were no events. She says she feels much better and is drinking well. She has had no nausea or vomiting since yesterday morning and no diarrhea since last night. She denies dizziness, abdominal pain, and trouble passing urine. Her only chronic condition is hypertension, and her home lisinopril has been held since admission. She is receiving normal saline at 100 mL per hour.

Vitals this morning are temperature 98.2 F, heart rate 78, blood pressure 118/70, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Her mucous membranes are now moist, the abdomen is soft and nontender, and she is no longer orthostatic. Urine output was good overnight. Creatinine is 1.5 today, down from 2.3 on admission and 0.9 at baseline, BUN 34, and potassium 4.2. Urinalysis was bland and a bladder scan showed a residual of 40 mL.

Impression is acute kidney injury from dehydration, improving with fluids. Plan is to stop the IV fluids this afternoon if she keeps drinking, keep lisinopril on hold until creatinine returns to baseline, avoid NSAIDs, and repeat a basic metabolic panel in the morning. If creatinine continues to fall, she can go home tomorrow with outpatient follow-up in one week.

Doctor: Good morning. I see you're a 79-year-old female here for your lung cancer follow-up and your next pembrolizumab infusion. How have you been feeling?
Patient: Pretty good, doctor. A little tired, but nothing new.
Doctor: Any fever, diarrhea, rash, or new cough since the last treatment?
Patient: No fever, no diarrhea, no rash, and no new cough.
Doctor: Good. I noticed on your chart that you haven't picked up your tiotropium inhaler in two months. What happened?
Patient: It costs too much every month. I've been using it only every other day to make it last, and some days I skip it.
Doctor: I'm glad you told me. Is your breathing worse because of that?
Patient: A bit winded on the stairs, but no chest pain.
Doctor: Okay. Your oxygen level is 95 percent. I hear mild wheezing in your lungs but no crackles. The scan from last month shows the tumor has shrunk, so the pembrolizumab 200 mg every three weeks is working.
Patient: That's a relief.
Doctor: My impression is that the lung cancer is responding well, and your COPD is a little worse because you've been rationing the inhaler. We will give your pembrolizumab today. I'll refer you to our financial counselor and social worker about copay assistance, and I'll ask the pharmacy about a lower-cost option. Please take the tiotropium 18 mcg once daily as prescribed. We'll do blood work today and repeat a CT scan in six weeks.
Patient: Thank you. I'll do that.
Doctor: Good. I'll see you in three weeks.

note:
Hospital day 3, postoperative day 2 progress note for a 46-year-old female who underwent a total laparoscopic hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for symptomatic uterine fibroids with heavy menstrual bleeding. The oophorectomy was performed for risk reduction because she is a BRCA1 mutation carrier.

Since surgery she has had marked hot flashes, about 8 to 10 a day, and drenching night sweats that wake her three times a night. She rates her distress from these symptoms as 7 out of 10. Her incisional pain is controlled and she is walking in the hallway, tolerating a regular diet, and passing flatus. She denies chest pain, calf pain or leg swelling, shortness of breath, fever, and heavy vaginal bleeding. She has no personal history of breast cancer or blood clots, and she does not smoke.

Current medications are acetaminophen 1000 mg every 6 hours and enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily. She received ketorolac 15 mg IV every 6 hours for the first 48 hours, which was stopped this morning, and we started ibuprofen 600 mg by mouth every 6 hours as needed instead.

Vitals this morning are temperature 98.6 F, heart rate 84, blood pressure 122/74, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Hemoglobin is 11.2 compared with 12.6 before surgery, and white count is 9.1. On exam she is comfortable, the lungs are clear, the abdomen is soft with appropriate incisional tenderness, the laparoscopic port sites are clean and dry, and the calves are soft and nontender.

Impression is expected recovery after hysterectomy with oophorectomy, complicated by surgical menopause with severe vasomotor symptoms. Because she has no breast cancer, no clotting history, and no uterus, estrogen-only therapy is appropriate until the usual age of natural menopause, and I discussed the benefits and risks with her. I am starting a transdermal estradiol patch 0.05 mg per 24 hours, changed twice weekly. Continue acetaminophen and enoxaparin, with ibuprofen as needed for pain. Advised layered clothing and avoiding hot triggers. Pathology is pending, and a baseline bone density scan will be arranged as an outpatient. Plan for discharge tomorrow if pain remains controlled, with a postoperative clinic visit in two weeks.

Her mother reports that overnight she slept in short stretches because of nasal congestion and a wet cough, but had no pauses in breathing, no color change, and no vomiting. She took about 70 percent of her usual breast milk volume overnight, up from 50 percent yesterday, and had four wet diapers in the past 12 hours. She had a low-grade fever on admission but has had none since. She was born at term and is otherwise healthy and up to date on vaccines, and her mother denies diarrhea and rash.

Background from admission: four days of runny nose, cough, fast breathing, and poor feeding. In the ED, one albuterol 2.5 mg nebulizer treatment produced no improvement and was not continued, per guideline. Visit modality: audio-only telephone visit with the patient at home. Verbal consent for telephone care was obtained and identity was verified. No video or photographs were available, so no visual examination was performed.

Reason for visit: follow-up of acne vulgaris in a 25-year-old female.

History reported by patient: She has had inflammatory acne for about 18 months, with red bumps and pustules mainly along the jawline, chin, and cheeks, plus a few tender deep bumps that flare in the week before her period. She says the acne has plateaued rather than improved over the last 3 months and is leaving dark marks. She has been using tretinoin 0.025% cream every night, benzoyl peroxide 5% wash once daily, and doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for the last 3 months. She reports mild dryness from the tretinoin but no burning. She denies nausea, heartburn, or pain with swallowing on the doxycycline, and has not had sun sensitivity or a rash. She also denies migraines with aura, calf pain or swelling, and has never smoked. She has never had a blood clot. She is sexually active with one partner and uses condoms only, and she would like something that treats the acne and also provides contraception. She has no known drug allergies.

Home measurements and results: blood pressure on her home cuff this morning was 112/68 with a pulse of 70. A home urine pregnancy test yesterday was negative. Labs from her last primary care visit 3 weeks ago showed ALT 24 and potassium 4.1.

Impression: acne vulgaris, moderate inflammatory type with perimenstrual flares, only partly controlled on topical therapy plus an oral antibiotic. She also has post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and mild retinoid dryness. Doctor: Good morning. I have your referral here for widespread pain. You're a 63-year-old male, correct? Tell me what's been going on.
Patient: Yeah. For about two years now I hurt all over. My neck, shoulders, back, hips, even my hands feel sore. I wake up exhausted no matter how long I sleep, and my brain feels foggy. I forget words in the middle of sentences.
Doctor: Does anything make it better or worse?
Patient: Cold weather and stress make it worse. A hot shower helps a little.
Doctor: Any swelling or redness in your joints, morning stiffness that lasts more than an hour, rashes, or dry eyes?
Patient: No swelling that I can see, the stiffness wears off in about twenty minutes, no rashes, and my eyes are fine.
Doctor: Any fever, weight loss, or weakness in your arms or legs?
Patient: No fever, I've actually put on a few pounds, and no weakness. My muscles just ache.
Doctor: What medicines are you taking right now?
Patient: Lisinopril 20 mg every morning for blood pressure, metformin 500 mg twice a day for my sugar, omeprazole 20 mg every morning for reflux, and duloxetine 60 mg once a day that my primary care doctor started four months ago. And ibuprofen, I take 800 mg three times a day for the pain.
Doctor: Eight hundred, three times a day, is a lot for over the counter. Can you check the bottle?
Patient: Hold on, sorry, correction. It's the 200 mg tablets. I take two at a time, so 400 mg, about twice a day.
Doctor: Okay, that's 400 mg twice a day, thank you. And how much do you drink?
Patient: A couple of beers a night, I'd say.
Doctor: I want to be sure about this because it matters for your medicines and your liver.
Patient: Honestly, it's closer to six beers a night, and more on weekends. It helps me fall asleep.
Doctor: Thanks for being honest. Do you snore?
Patient: My wife says I snore loudly and stop breathing sometimes, but I've never had a sleep study.
Doctor: Alright. Your blood pressure today is 138 over 84, pulse 78, weight 94 kilograms. On exam you have tenderness over many soft-tissue points at the neck, shoulders, chest wall, and hips, but there is no joint swelling, your strength is normal, and your range of motion is full. Your labs from last week: ESR 12, CRP 2, TSH 2.1, CK 110, hemoglobin 14.2, vitamin D 22, A1c 6.8, AST 58 and ALT 41. The ANA, rheumatoid factor, and anti-CCP are all negative. X-rays of your hands and neck showed only mild arthritis changes.
Patient: So what is it?
Doctor: This is fibromyalgia, in a man who also has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and reflux. Nothing here points to rheumatoid arthritis or lupus. The AST being higher than the ALT, along with the heavy drinking, makes me think alcohol is affecting your liver, and your drinking is heavy enough that I would call it alcohol use disorder. Heavy drinking also worsens sleep quality and pain.
Doctor: Here's the plan. First, stop the ibuprofen. NSAIDs are a bad idea with your blood pressure, kidneys, and drinking, and they don't help fibromyalgia. Second, duloxetine is not a good fit with heavy alcohol use and a high AST, so lower it to 30 mg daily for one week, then stop. Third, start gabapentin 100 mg at bedtime and we'll increase it slowly, but you can't drink with it because it adds to the drowsiness. Fourth, acetaminophen 500 mg up to twice a day if needed, never more than 2 grams a day. Fifth, vitamin D3 2,000 units daily. I'm referring you to physical therapy for a graded exercise program, to cognitive behavioral therapy, to addiction medicine for the drinking, and for a sleep study. We'll repeat liver tests in six weeks, and I'll see you back in eight weeks.
Patient: Okay, I'll give it a go.

summary: An 87-year-old male with hyperlipidemia reported six months of right calf cramping after walking about a block that resolves with a couple of minutes of rest. He denied pain at night, foot sores, numbness, chest pain and shortness of breath, though his feet sometimes feel cold. Ankle and foot pulses were faint with cool, shiny, hairless skin and no ulcers, and the ankle-brachial index was 0.62 on the right and 0.71 on the left. The impression was peripheral artery disease with claudication, mild and stable. Plan is to continue aspirin and atorvastatin, a walking program, daily foot checks, return precautions, and follow-up in three months.

soap.assessment: Peripheral artery disease with claudication, mild and stable, so no procedure is needed now. Hyperlipidemia.

Walk on a flat surface for 30 minutes three times a week, resting when calf pain starts and resuming when it eases
Check feet daily and wear well-fitting shoes
Call for pain at rest, a sore that does not heal, or a cold, pale foot
Follow-up in three months

Doctor: Hi there. Let's see, you're a 40-year-old female, and you came in to get your diabetes checked and your refills?
Patient: Yes. I missed my last two appointments at my regular clinic because I don't have a car and the bus takes almost two hours each way. So I figured I'd come here today.
Doctor: I'm glad you did. How have you been feeling?
Patient: Really thirsty all the time, I'm going to the bathroom a lot, and I'm tired by the afternoon.
Doctor: Any vomiting, belly pain, blurry vision, or numbness or tingling in your feet?
Patient: No vomiting, no belly pain, my vision is okay, and my feet feel normal.
Doctor: Any chest pain or trouble breathing?
Patient: No.
Doctor: What medicines are you taking?
Patient: Metformin 1000 mg twice a day, and lisinopril 10 mg once a day for blood pressure. I take them every day, except I ran out of metformin last week.
Doctor: Okay. Your A1c from the lab last week came back at 8.9, up from 7.4 six months ago. Your fingerstick sugar here today is 248. Your blood pressure is 132/84, pulse 82, and weight 96 kilograms. Your kidney function is fine, creatinine 0.8 and eGFR 98. I checked your feet with the monofilament and the sensation is normal.
Patient: That's not good, is it?
Doctor: It's higher than we want, but we can fix it. My impression is type 2 diabetes that's not at goal, mostly because of the missed refills and visits, and also hypertension that is slightly above goal. Here's the plan. Restart the metformin 1000 mg twice a day today and start empagliflozin 10 mg once a day in the morning. It can cause genital yeast infections, so keep the area clean and drink plenty of water. Continue the lisinopril 10 mg daily. I'll send all prescriptions as 90-day supplies to a mail-order pharmacy that delivers to your home, so you don't need a ride for refills. We'll do your follow-up visits by phone or video every 4 to 6 weeks, and I'll have the repeat A1c done at the lab near your home in three months. Your insurance also covers rides to medical visits, and our staff will give you the number to call.
Patient: Thank you, that helps a lot.

A1c rose from 7.4 to 8.9, fingerstick glucose was 248, blood pressure 132/84, creatinine 0.8, and the foot monofilament exam was normal. The impression was type 2 diabetes not at goal with hypertension slightly above goal. Plan is to restart metformin, start empagliflozin 10 mg daily, continue lisinopril, mail-order 90-day supplies, telehealth follow-ups, and a repeat A1c in three months.

Doctor: Good afternoon. You're a 55-year-old female, referred because your calcium came back high on routine blood work. Tell me how you've been feeling.
Patient: Honestly I've been exhausted for a year or more, and I get constipated a lot. My bones ache, especially my hips and lower back, and I'm up peeing at night.
Doctor: Any nausea, vomiting, confusion, or belly pain?
Patient: No nausea, no vomiting, no confusion. My stomach is fine.
Doctor: Any broken bones, or kidney stones?
Patient: No fractures, but I passed a kidney stone about two years ago.
Doctor: What medications do you take?
Patient: Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg every morning for blood pressure, calcium carbonate 500 mg twice a day, and vitamin D3 1,000 units daily.
Doctor: And alcohol?
Patient: I have four or five glasses of wine a night. I know it's a lot.
Doctor: Thanks for telling me. That is heavy alcohol use, and it matters for your bones and for dehydration. Your blood pressure today is 148/88 and pulse 76. Your labs show calcium 11.4, PTH 96, phosphorus 2.4, creatinine 0.9, eGFR 78, and vitamin D 24. Your 24-hour urine calcium was 320 mg. The bone density scan shows a T-score of -2.7 at the forearm, which is osteoporosis.
Patient: What does that mean?
Doctor: You have primary hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcemia. One of your parathyroid glands is overactive and pulling calcium out of your bones. With your kidney stone and the bone loss, I recommend surgery to remove it. Hydrochlorothiazide can raise calcium, and since your hypertension needs treatment, we'll stop it and start amlodipine 5 mg daily. Stop the calcium carbonate, and increase vitamin D3 to 2,000 units daily. Drink plenty of water, and please cut back on the wine. I'm ordering an ultrasound of the neck and a sestamibi scan to locate the gland, and I'm referring you to endocrine surgery. We'll repeat calcium and PTH in four weeks, and I'll see you back in six weeks.
Patient: Okay, I'll do that.
summary: A 55-year-old female was referred to endocrinology for hypercalcemia found on routine labs, with a year of fatigue, constipation, bone aches and nighttime urination, a kidney stone two years ago, and four to five glasses of wine nightly. She denied nausea, vomiting, confusion and fractures. Blood pressure was 148/88, calcium 11.4, PTH 96, creatinine 0.9, 24-hour urine calcium 320 mg, and a bone density scan showed a forearm T-score of -2.7. The impression was primary hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcemia and osteoporosis. Plan is to switch hydrochlorothiazide to amlodipine, stop calcium carbonate, increase vitamin D3, order a neck ultrasound and sestamibi scan, refer to endocrine surgery, and counsel on alcohol reduction.
